documents: Autin et al. 2022, JGR Atmospheres 127, e2021JD035410 (published paper, PDF)

entry.evidence: Several studies put forward different atmospheric/meteorological factors as being responsible for the interannual variability of the surface mass balance of tropical glaciers in the Andes

steps.action: Posed the question of which atmospheric and meteorological factors control the interseasonal and interannual surface mass-balance variability of Zongo Glacier, using a nine-year distributed energy-balance modelling run.
steps.quote: we applied DEBAM to Zongo Glacier over nine years to obtain deeper insights

steps.action: Took candidate controls from the literature: the onset of the wet season or transition period (Sicart et al. 2011), ENSO, air temperature, and moisture-related variables such as precipitation, albedo and cloudiness.
steps.quote: Some highlighted the importance of the onset of the wet season

steps.action: Analysed the 1992-2017 monthly stake mass-balance record of the ablation zone and found the largest and most variable losses from September to November.
steps.quote: We analyzed the mass-balance record (1992–2017, Vincent et al., 2018) to characterize the glaciological regime

steps.action: Correlated annual mass balance with incoming shortwave and longwave radiation (R2 = 0.28 and 0.0) and with air temperature (glacier-wide R2 = 0.18), finding weak relations.
steps.quote: We correlated monthly mass balances to monthly mean air temperatures at the on-glacier weather station (SAMA)

steps.action: Computed monthly probability density functions of cloud radiative forcing over 13 years and showed that they distinguish the transition, wet and dry seasons.
steps.quote: cloud radiative forcing is distinctly different for the core wet season (January–March), the dry season (June–August) and the transition period

steps.action: Set up DEBAM at hourly resolution on a 20 x 20 m grid, forced with gap-filled SAMA AWS data and ultrasonic-gauge precipitation, with a DEM interpolated for each year.
steps.quote: We apply the open-source mass-balance model DEBAM

steps.action: Compared runs on annually adjusted DEMs with runs on the constant 1997 DEM; the adjusted DEMs raised R2 against observed balances from 0.5 to 0.84.
steps.quote: Accounting for the glacier retreat improved the correlation

steps.action: Calibrated one parameter set for all nine years: albedo parameters from SAMA albedo in two contrasting years, and roughness length from June 2011 eddy-covariance data.
steps.quote: The albedo was calibrated using measurements at SAMA for two contrasting years

steps.action: Validated the model against held-out years (albedo), 2007 eddy-covariance data (roughness), TUBO discharge, snow-line photographs and stake mass-balance profiles; reported mismatches, including dry-season discharge overestimation and a 0.18 m w.e. mean overestimate of mass loss.
steps.quote: To validate model performances, we focus on the following observations

steps.action: Designed precipitation scenarios S1-S3, which reshuffle whole days of transition-season forcing (thresholds 2 and 9 mm/d) while conserving precipitation totals, and cloud scenarios that impose 66th-percentile cloud forcing over September, October or November.
steps.quote: We perform a series of sensitivity experiments to analyze the impact of the timing of precipitation amounts

steps.action: Estimated glacier-wide annual mass balance, melt and monthly energy fluxes for the nine years from the reference runs (Table 3, Figure 7).
steps.quote: Simulated annual glacier-wide surface mass balances range between 0.49 and −1.90 m w.e.

steps.action: Compared three low-loss years with three high-loss years on precipitation, albedo and cloud index; found higher albedo in the low-loss years during the transition period, and annual balance well correlated with net shortwave radiation (R2 = 0.84).
steps.quote: [...] limited net mass loss: 1999/2000, 2000/2001, and 2005/2006 were compared to three years with high mass loss

steps.action: Set conditions in the model: swapped transition-season forcing between 2004/2005 and 2005/2006 (annual loss changed by 1.18 and 1.00 m w.e.), and ran scenarios S1-S3 for three contrasting years.
steps.quote: we carried out model runs where the data of the transition season of a year with limited mass loss

steps.action: Compared the scenario runs with the reference runs: spreading the events evenly (S1, S2) raised albedo and lowered melt, while grouping them (S3) raised melt, with year-dependent exceptions such as 2004/2005.
steps.quote: scenarios S1 and S2 reduced the melt rate by 7% and 2%, respectively, whilst scenario S3 increased the melt rate by 12%

steps.action: Applied scenario S1 to all nine years: mass loss fell by 0.06 m w.e. on average, more in wet years than in dry years, with a negligible effect where events were already evenly spread.
steps.quote: we applied this scenario to all nine simulated years

steps.action: Compared the cloud-scenario runs with the reference runs: sustained cloud cover reduced transition-period melt by 6%, 15% and 20% for September, October and November.
steps.quote: the melt rate over the transition period decreased by 6%, 15%, and 20% in the September, October, and November scenarios respectively

steps.action: Checked the premise of the cloud-scenario method: the loss of physical coherence changed turbulent fluxes by at most -5% relative to the reference runs.
steps.quote: This confirms that the loss of coherence between measured parameters in the cloud scenarios has a small impact

steps.action: Kept the claim that the temporal distribution of precipitation drives interannual mass-balance variability through the albedo feedback, together with the role of October-November and of the wet-season onset.
steps.quote: validated the hypothesis that the frequency of precipitation events is a key driver of the interannual variability of the surface mass balance

tree.answer: Interannual and seasonal variability of Zongo Glacier surface mass balance, largest in the transition period
Mass balance is observed directly; the energy fluxes are inferred through DEBAM
Identify the climate controls on mass-balance variability
Air temperature, ENSO, wet-season onset or transition period, precipitation timing and amount, cloud cover
Partly: model scenarios that shuffle precipitation timing and impose cloud forcing
Conditions set inside the model by reshuffled and rescaled forcing

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nine natural years are compared as repeated cases (low-loss vs high-loss years)
Threshold variant (S2), S1 applied to all nine years, turbulent-flux coherence check
Kept: precipitation timing, through the albedo feedback, is a key driver

end.claim: The temporal distribution of precipitation events, especially in October-November, is a key driver of the interannual variability of Zongo Glacier's surface mass balance through an albedo feedback on net shortwave radiation.

decisive_move.sentence: The precipitation-reshuffling scenarios, which conserve totals and change only timing, isolate the effect of event distribution on melt; without them the timing claim would rest on correlation alone.

gates.evidence: The data come from a long-term monitoring program, not acquisition directed by a hypothesis. The scenario experiments could have shown no effect of precipitation timing, but they run within the same model calibrated on the same data. No hypothesis, analysis or threshold was fixed before the data were seen: the S1 threshold was chosen on physical grounds (1 cm of snow) and S1 was selected for the nine-year run after the three-year results.

imports.item: Probability density functions and correlation analysis of cloud radiative forcing and mass balance

novelty_claims.quote: The long data set available at Zongo Glacier provides a unique opportunity to investigate the climate factors
we found that three seasons (wet, dry, and transition) can be identified based on the cloud radiative properties

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: seasons defined by cloud radiative forcing (regularity_in_range, 13 years at one site); the transition period controls the annual balance (best_explanation, from model fluxes and the season-swap runs); sustained clouds in November reduce melt most (estimate_with_resolution in the model; the authors say it is probably underestimated because added precipitation is ignored). All causal tests are in-model. The model was calibrated on two of the nine years and on the AWS data that also force it, so the experiments test the model's own sensitivities rather than independent data. Inference: the S1 threshold choice and the selection of S1 for the nine-year run came after the three-year results, so the analysis path was not fixed in advance. No review file was supplied, so the process changes made in review are unknown. Composition is none_fits: the walk combines found repetitions across nine natural years with conditions set inside a model (model-based intervention). It fits neither natures_repetition (conditions are set) nor trace_series or strong_inference (no shared crucial test among rivals; ENSO and air-temperature rivals are only addressed by weak correlations).

disagreements.target: Bradley et al. (2009) temperature-mass balance correlations for Quelccaya
disagreements.support: Citing Gurgiser et al. (2013), the paper argues that the correlations reflect temperature's effect on precipitation phase; its own temperature correlation with the glacier-wide balance is low (R2 = 0.18).
disagreements.quote: these might result from the indirect effect of air temperature on the phase of precipitation

disagreements.target: Previous season classifications based on mass balance (Rabatel et al., 2012, 2013) or on precipitation and melt (Sicart et al., [...]
disagreements.support: Monthly PDFs of cloud radiative forcing over 13 years separate the three seasons.
disagreements.quote: In contrast to previous classifications based on surface mass balance variations (e.g., Rabatel et al., 2012, 2013)

Precipitation threshold of 2 mm/d for scenario S1
alternatives_considered.reason: 2 mm/d allows at least 1 cm of snow and so changes albedo; S2 tests the threshold impact

alternatives_considered.chosen: Energy fluxes analysed at the AWS
alternatives_considered.reason: Avoid simulation errors from spatial extrapolation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Scenario S1 applied to all nine years
alternatives_considered.reason: S1 generated the largest reduction in melt over the transition period
